title: Calling on School Leaders to Disable YouTube and Gemini AI on School-Issued Devices
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin reports that she and twelve other organizations and experts sent an open letter to the 150 largest US school districts asking them to disable YouTube and Gemini AI on school-issued devices. She argues that recent jury verdicts and district lawsuits against YouTube, plus suits over Chromebooks and Chrome, show that harms to children are documented and that technology companies will shift legal risk onto the districts. The post reproduces her own email to Seattle Public Schools leaders, which lists three requested steps: disable YouTube, disable Gemini, and investigate and publicly report student internet use on district devices. She notes an internal audit reportedly found about 2,000 EdTech products in use in Seattle. Her closing claim is that children need technology education rather than technology products, and that the best preparation for a digital future is a primarily analog childhood.
points: The letter asks districts to take three concrete steps: disable YouTube, disable Gemini AI, and audit and publish student internet use on school devices.
Cherkin frames inaction as a choice, warning that when lawsuits arrive the technology companies will push legal risk onto the district.
An internal audit reportedly found about 2,000 EdTech products or apps in use in Seattle, a number she calls astonishingly high.
She distinguishes technology education, which children need, from technology products, which mostly serve company profit.
quotes: A California jury found that YouTube is “dangerous or likely to be dangerous to minors when used in a reasonably foreseeable way,” and even awarded punitive damages against YouTube for acting with “malice, oppression, or fraud.
Yet many of these same very school districts still allow their students access to YouTube on school-issued devices.

Our goal in sending this letter is to help school districts see that inaction is a choice— that when (not if) lawsuits occur in their districts because children are experiencing harms on the devices they provide, Google and other technology companies will shift legal risks onto the district.
It is my understanding that an internal audit in Seattle Public Schools found there are currently 2,000 EdTech products or apps in use. This is an astonishingly high number.
but technology companies need children to be profitable. The best preparation for a digital future is a primarily analog childhood and education.

Seattle has the potential to be a leader in doing the right thing by children and our district should not be acquiescing to pressure from technology companies who prey on vulnerable institutions and populations.
